title: The presentation of self in the age of ChatGPT
author: Nils Klowait · Maria Erofeeva

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The supplied source material contains only bibliographic references and no attributable substantive claims, evidence or reasoning. Its position on whether AI-assisted productivity gains translate into employment, income or learning outcomes therefore cannot be determined.

st.t: Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status
st.an: The supplied source summary contains only bibliographic references and no substantive claims, findings, reasoning, predictions or recommendations. There is therefore insufficient evidence to determine its position on whether AI redistributes legal tasks and professional status through organisational choices and contested professional power.

st.t: AI writing: Present gains can weaken future judgment
st.an: The source accepts supervised AI augmentation and verification, then materially extends the cluster by examining how AI-assisted writing affects authorship, professional identity and accountability. It proposes concrete provenance and human-oversight conventions, while treating its employment and identity implications as exploratory rather than measured findings.
qs: We checked citations, worried about unintentional plagiarism and fretted over whether the prose still “sounded like us.” We made sure that nothing was copy-pasted, and that AI contributions were only initial drafts that augmented existing writing – and we made sure to point this out in the text.

Possibilities include journals requiring a “prompt provenance” section, universities teaching prompt literacy alongside citation ethics, or professional bodies demanding signed attestations of human oversight.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of task-level augmentation rather than wholesale lawyer replacement, while materially extending it by showing that workflow redesign also changes how competence, effort and credibility are made visible. It adds professional identity, concealed adoption and symbolic task significance as organisational risks alongside verification and capability concerns.
qs: An AI might take over specific tasks—like summarizing documents, coding routine functions, or drafting a first version of a legal brief—without supplanting the entire occupation.

While analyzing the current extent of workplace AI exposure, we must look at a profession’s multicomponent structure that not only includes different types of tasks (manual and cognitive, routine and non-routine), but also visible, invisible and hidden elements that bear symbolic meaning to performing professionals.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of selective, supplementary automation, human responsibility and work redesign. It materially extends that account by showing that task-level analysis can miss symbolic and relational labour through which professionals demonstrate competence, and by linking AI deployment to disclosure, identity, recognition and the quality of supervisory work.
qs: Drawing on Goffman’s dramaturgical sociology, this paper reframes AI in the workplace as *supplementary* rather than *substitutive* automation.
Analytically, it cautions against treating AI exposure as a simple task-substitution ratio; the dramaturgical functions of tasks must be considered alongside their technical content.

kp.k: Exploratory dramaturgical framework, not systematic empirical findings
kp.d: The authors apply Goffman’s sociology to workplace AI, drawing on anecdotes, auto-ethnographic reflections, public vignettes, industry reports and informal professional conversations. Legal work appears among broader examples of cognitive occupations. The paper’s propositions about visibility, professional identity and automation are an exploratory theoretical interpretation rather than findings from a systematic study of legal services.
qs: This article has been a thought experiment rather than an exhaustive empirical study or a heavyweight theoretical intervention.

Following Goffman’s footsteps, we will draw on a mix of field-inspired anecdotes, auto-ethnographic reflections, public vignettes, formal industry reports, and informal conversations with professionals who both deploy—and publicly defend—their use of artificial intelligence.

kp.k: Supplementary automation changes tasks without replacing whole occupations
kp.d: The authors argue that contemporary AI increasingly accommodates messy human workflows and selectively takes over components of jobs, rather than requiring entirely rationalized environments that permit wholesale substitution. Summarizing documents and drafting legal briefs illustrate this supplementary mode. They nevertheless warn that task consolidation can eliminate jobs even when systems cannot match workers’ overall abilities; supplementation is not a guarantee of employment security.
qs: An AI might take over specific tasks—like summarizing documents, coding routine functions, or drafting a first version of a legal brief—without supplanting the entire occupation.

Yet if we shift our attention to a contemporary AI’s capacity to chip away at the total workload of a given worker, we can appreciate that many persons can lose their job to systems that are substantially less performant than the average human.

kp.k: Professional competence requires symbolic work as well as delivery
kp.d: Drawing on Goffman, the authors distinguish technical duties from the communicative work of making competence and dedication recognizable. Frontstage presentations depend on backstage activity that clients cannot directly observe. They argue that AI exposure assessments must consider tasks’ visibility and symbolic significance alongside their cognitive, manual, routine or non-routine character, rather than treating impression management merely as deception or profit maximization.
qs: It means that workers do not only stage their work efforts for the sake of maximizing profit.

The dramaturgical perspective transforms our view on automation prevalent both in public discourse and in many scientific reports: it is not only about what is actually done; it is also about what is made visible.

kp.k: Hidden AI use can protect status and remuneration
kp.d: An author’s account of discovering improved Russian-English Google Translate in 2016 illustrates partial automation followed by continued human editing and checking. The authors use it to ask whether professionals would disclose efficiency gains, lower prices, or instead emphasize technological limitations. More broadly, they interpret concealment of AI assistance as a possible response to threats to occupational status and compensation, not as an empirically established pricing response by lawyers.
qs: They are still necessary for now—as editors, double-checkers, refiners, managers.
Will they ask for less money in the future?
Luckily to the affected, exactly because such routines are invisible, their automation is easier to hide.

kp.k: Survey discrepancies suggest potentially concealed workplace adoption
kp.d: The article reports Mayer et al. (2025) as finding that three times more employees use generative AI for at least one-third of daily work tasks than superiors assume. It also reports that nearly half of respondents want formal training and that 71% affirm their organizations will deploy AI ethically. The authors interpret these responses as potentially strategic presentations by workers and leadership; concealment and conformity are their interpretations, not independently demonstrated survey mechanisms.
qs: Nearly half of the respondents expressed a desire for more formal training.

This may explain the results obtained by McKinsey Institute ([Mayer et al., 2025](#ref29)) that three times more employees are using generative AI for their daily work tasks than their employers think.

kp.k: Professional communities collectively defend expertise and entry barriers
kp.d: The authors extend impression management from individuals to professional teams and fields. Communities develop certifications, defend reputations and may conceal technologies that reduce skill requirements. Drawing on Goffman’s pharmacist example, they argue that lengthy education can serve the presentation of difficult-to-obtain expertise as well as functional training. This is a general sociological argument, not a finding about the appropriate duration of legal education.
qs: He argues that one reason for ‘years of schooling’ is not just functional necessity (time to acquire sufficient levels of competence), but rather part of a performance of professionalism.
They will develop professional certifications, resist scandals, and will hide when a technology makes their work easier (and thereby possibly lowering the skill requirements to accomplish it).

kp.k: Legal backstage automation destabilizes traditional evidence of diligence
kp.d: The authors identify document summarization, first-pass translation, contract boilerplate and synthetic literature reviews as mundane but cognitively demanding tasks where LLMs have a comparative advantage. In their legal illustrations, discovery work and precedent preparation support courtroom displays of competence. Automating such work weakens familiar signals of effort, prompting professionals to seek alternative demonstrations of expertise. These are illustrative mechanisms, not measured legal productivity results.
qs: LLMs demonstrate their greatest comparative advantage in tasks that are simultaneously mundane and cognitively demanding: summarizing voluminous documents, producing first-pass translations, drafting contract boiler-plate or generating synthetic literature reviews.
The immediate dramaturgical effect is to render traditional markers of diligence—stacked files, annotated drafts, late-night office lights—anachronistic.
Professionals must therefore search for replacement cues capable of reproducing a semblance of industrious depth.

kp.k: Digital scrutiny creates additional documentation and disclosure work
kp.d: The authors argue that AI-assisted documents face multiple, sometimes asynchronous audiences: models, platform filters, clients, supervisors and later auditors. A document initially accepted may subsequently attract scrutiny, creating incentives to preserve prompts, identify model versions and add human commentary. Such practices are presented as emerging forms of professional self-presentation rather than established legal compliance requirements.
qs: A polished memo produced with AI help may sail through managerial approval only to be flagged weeks later by a plagiarism detector or a governance audit.

Consequently, workers engage in preventive facework reminiscent of Goffman’s “make-work” practices, but updated for the age of digital traceability: they may archive prompt histories, cite model versions, or interleave human commentary that reiterates professional norms.

kp.k: Verification and accountability may become professional differentiators
kp.d: The authors predict that distinctively human contributions may shift partly toward empathy, judgment, detecting fabricated output and accepting responsibility. Visible assurances of human verification could replace displays of unaided craft. They caution that these contributions may be difficult to demonstrate and undervalued, drawing an analogy with nursing’s relational work. Their workshop anecdote further illustrates how assurances of vigilance can themselves express professional status rather than establish actual checking behavior.
qs: In professional services the analogous premium now attaches to judgemental empathy: the capacity to translate client anxieties into bespoke prompts, to sense when factual hallucinations might slip through, or to shoulder accountability for decisions that no model can own.
When we suggested that fatigue, deadlines, and ambient chaos might erode that vigilance, they doubled down:
The risk is that what remains human becomes, ironically, what institutions undervalue.

kp.k: AI-assisted authorship exposes tensions over professional ownership
kp.d: The authors deliberately used frontier models throughout the paper’s production as a reflexive experiment, including for literature reviews, drafting, feedback, summaries and translation. They distinguish relatively comfortable assistance, such as spelling correction and transcription, from generating arguments and sections that threatened their sense of authorship. The disclosure states that generated output was not used verbatim or one-shot and assigns ultimate responsibility to the human authors.
qs: We found ourselves hoping the model would hallucinate, so that our corrective labor could restore a sense of authorship.
In short, we could take ownership of AI work by highlighting our own contributions to it.
Generative output was never used verbatim or one-shot, with long chains of feedback and editing.
Ultimate responsibility rests, and can only ever rest, with the humans listed as the paper’s authors.

kp.k: Published outputs can misrepresent what occupations actually require
kp.d: The authors argue that models trained on polished public-facing material reproduce professional styles while missing private coordination, emotional labor and troubleshooting. They warn that executives may mistake replication of visible outputs for replacement of whole occupations and remove workers whose less visible contributions sustain organizations. This is their theoretical warning about training-data and managerial distortions, not an empirical demonstration of particular layoffs.
qs: They therefore reproduce front-stage stylistics with uncanny fidelity while remaining largely blind to backstage coordination, emotional labor and informal troubleshooting.
When senior executives hail GPT-style systems as replacements for engineers or researchers, they may be grossly underestimating the dramaturgical distortions of the training data that underpins LLMs.

kp.k: AI disclosure costs follow institutional power differences
kp.d: The meta-conclusion contrasts authors’ exposure to scrutiny with potentially less visible AI use by reviewers and publishers. The authors argue that people can be subjected to AI through others’ decisions, while challenging that use can be professionally costly. They hypothesize that gender, race, age and class will also shape these costs, and call for systematic comparative research rather than claiming demonstrated distributional effects.
qs: AI is not simply a thing that people may choose to use, but can also be a thing that happens *to* them externally.
It appears highly probable that structural inequalities across gender, race, age, class will modulate dramaturgical cost associated with AI, and may represent another shadow cost of work.

kp.k: Governance should recognize oversight, responsibility and remuneration
kp.d: The authors suggest prompt provenance disclosures, teaching prompt literacy alongside citation ethics, and signed attestations of human oversight as possible new professional conventions. They recommend organizational recognition and spaces for controlled disclosure, while arguing that labor law and professional licensure must address authorship, liability and remuneration in hybrid work. These are proposals, not descriptions of adopted professional rules; the principal risk they emphasize is degraded, undercompensated human supervision.
qs: Possibilities include journals requiring a “prompt provenance” section, universities teaching prompt literacy alongside citation ethics, or professional bodies demanding signed attestations of human oversight.
If intellectual work increasingly depends on hybrid human-AI teams, labor law and professional licensure must grapple with issues of authorship, liability and remuneration.
Without intervention, the danger is not a jobless future but a future of degraded work in which humans perform high-stakes supervision without commensurate recognition or pay.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Klowait and Erofeeva argue that AI primarily automates components of knowledge work rather than replacing entire occupations, while changing how professionals demonstrate competence.
pts.d: This cross-domain article addresses cognitive occupations, including law, translation, journalism and academic research. The authors describe LLMs taking over backstage activities such as summarization, translation, first drafts and contract boilerplate. Humans retain visible, relational and supervisory responsibilities but must find new ways to signal diligence and expertise. The legal examples are illustrations of this argument, not reported studies of legal practice.

pts.k: The authors argue that professional status and income concerns encourage workers to conceal AI assistance or emphasize its limitations.
pts.d: They interpret discrepancies between employee-reported adoption and managerial estimates as potentially reflecting impression management. Professional communities may likewise protect their standing by downplaying technological assistance. This is an interpretive explanation rather than a demonstrated causal finding. Their translator anecdote raises possible pressure on fees but does not establish actual fee reductions.

pts.k: Supplementary automation can still eliminate jobs through consolidation and can degrade remaining work.
pts.d: Klowait and Erofeeva distinguish partial task automation from job security: a system need not match a whole human occupation to reduce staffing needs. They reject an assumption that all saved effort can be redirected into additional demand or reliably paid creative work. Their longer-term concern is insufficiently recognized and compensated human supervision, rather than necessarily universal unemployment.

pts.k: Human value may shift toward empathy, verification and accountability, while AI-related scrutiny creates additional work around disclosure and digital records.
pts.d: The authors predict a partial shift from linguistic craft toward understanding clients, detecting fabricated content and accepting responsibility. They distinguish the actual work of checking output from public demonstrations of responsibility, suggesting that both become professionally significant. They also describe possible defensive practices such as retaining prompts and recording model versions. These claims are theoretical and illustrative, not quantified changes in legal workflows.

pts.k: Organizations may damage professional cooperation and trust if they treat polished AI outputs as substitutes for the full work behind them.
pts.d: The authors argue that models reproduce public-facing genres without necessarily capturing private coordination, emotional labor or troubleshooting. They warn that layoffs based on visible output capabilities can remove essential hidden labor. They propose, rather than report adoption of, new conventions such as prompt provenance, prompt literacy and signed human-oversight attestations.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal basis is exploratory sociological argument supported by personal experience, illustrative anecdotes, existing scholarship and industry reports.
pts.d: The authors use Goffman’s dramaturgical framework, a co-author’s experience with Russian–English machine translation, their own intensive AI-assisted writing process and an AI workshop with managers. They cite productivity research and industry adoption surveys, including Mayer et al. (2025), whose reported gap between employee use and employer perceptions they interpret as consistent with concealment. They also repeat WEF projections of 11 million jobs created and 9 million lost by 2030, and McKinsey estimates concerning affected working hours and occupational transitions. These are externally attributed estimates, not original measurements or legal-sector forecasts. No systematic legal-practice study or legal-task benchmark is presented.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The main argument concerns changes already underway at the time of writing in 2025; most prospective consequences have no fixed deadline.
pts.d: The historical translation example concerns Google Translate’s 2016 transition. Contemporary observations concern frontier LLMs available during manuscript preparation, including ChatGPT o3. The paper presents future changes in recognition, supervision, inequality and professional conventions as conditional possibilities. It explicitly qualifies replacement claims by acknowledging current model limitations and calling for systematic empirical research. The 2030 horizon belongs to the external WEF employment projection, not a prediction of lawyer replacement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The authors describe uneven effects across knowledge workers, managers, professional communities and audiences, with particular risks for precarious workers and undervalued relational roles.
pts.d: Lawyers illustrate changes in document preparation and demonstrations of diligence; translators illustrate threats to professional identity and pricing; academics illustrate authorship and disclosure pressures. Clients and supervisors must interpret changing signals of expertise and responsibility. The authors identify low- and middle-wage workers as especially exposed, drawing on external reports. They also suggest that institutional power and inequalities of gender, race, age and class will shape the burden of defending AI use. They do not differentiate legal effects by firm size, practice area, provider type or buyer segment.
